posts.title: Agent frameworks are dissolving
posts.hook: The agent framework you're evaluating today will be a built-in feature of the LLM provider by Q2.
posts.body:
The agent framework you're evaluating today will be a built-in feature of the LLM provider by Q2.

I watched this happen in real time with my own stack. Built a custom orchestration layer for multi-step enrichment workflows. Tool calls, retries, context threading, the whole thing. Took two weeks.

Then Anthropic shipped tool_use natively. Then extended thinking. Then the agent SDK.

Every layer I built got absorbed into the model provider itself.

The pattern is obvious if you've been building long enough: middleware gets eaten. LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen... they're all building on top of capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are shipping as primitives.

This doesn't mean frameworks are useless. It means the durable layer is your business logic, not your orchestration code. The enrichment pipeline I run daily doesn't care whether tool calls are routed through LangChain or native Claude tool_use. It cares about the data model, the scoring logic, the output schema.

So I stopped investing in orchestration abstractions. I write thin wrappers over native APIs. When the provider ships a better version of what I built, I delete my code and use theirs.

The founders who win here are the ones building domain-specific value on top, not the ones building generic plumbing underneath.

remixes.label: graveyard-of-abstractions
remixes.hook: I have a folder called 'deprecated' that tells the entire story of AI infrastructure in 2025.
remixes.body:
I have a folder called 'deprecated' that tells the entire story of AI infrastructure in 2025.

Inside it: a custom retry handler I wrote in March. A context window manager from April. A tool orchestration layer from May. A streaming parser from June.

Every single one was replaced by a native feature from the model provider within 90 days of me building it.

The pattern is predictable now. You identify a gap in the LLM's capabilities. You build a clever workaround. You get attached to your clever workaround. Then the provider ships it as a first-class feature that works better than yours because they have access to the model internals you were guessing at.

This isn't a complaint. It's a design principle. The only defensible layer in an AI stack is the one closest to your specific business logic. Everything else is a temporary shim.

I've stopped building anything that feels like "making the model work better." If I'm writing code that compensates for a model limitation, I put a six-week expiration date on it mentally. Because that limitation is on someone's roadmap right now.

The founders who are winning build thin. They treat the infrastructure layer as rented, not owned. Their code is 80% domain logic and 20% glue. When the glue becomes native, they just delete files.
remixes.cta: Look at your AI codebase. How much of it is domain logic vs. model compensation? That ratio tells you how much rework is coming.

remixes.label: build-to-delete
remixes.hook: The best AI engineering skill in 2025 isn't building. It's knowing what to delete.
remixes.body:
The best AI engineering skill in 2025 isn't building. It's knowing what to delete.

Last quarter I ripped out 1,200 lines of orchestration code. Not because it was broken. Because Claude's agent SDK made it redundant overnight. The code worked fine. It just wasn't necessary anymore.

Most teams can't do this. They spent months on their orchestration layer. They have tests for it. Documentation. A developer who "owns" it. Deleting it feels like admitting the work was wasted.

It wasn't wasted. It was scaffolding. And scaffolding comes down when the building stands on its own.

Here's what I tell founders who are deep in agent framework selection right now: pick the one that's easiest to remove. Not easiest to adopt. Easiest to remove. Because the half-life of any abstraction layer between your code and the model is about four months.

The teams shipping fastest have a weird discipline. They build every integration layer as if it's temporary. Minimal configuration. No custom DSLs. No framework-specific patterns leaking into business logic. When the provider absorbs the feature, they delete the file and move on.

Fragile architectures fight change. Antifragile architectures expect it.
remixes.cta: Next time you evaluate an agent framework, ask: how many lines of code does it take to fully remove this? That's your real switching cost.

posts.title: Claude Code speed gap is real
posts.hook: I timed myself building the same enrichment script in Claude Code vs. manually. 11 minutes vs. 2 hours.
posts.body:
I timed myself building the same enrichment script in Claude Code vs. manually. 11 minutes vs. 2 hours.

The script: pull a company list from Attio, hit an enrichment API, score results against ICP criteria, write back to CRM. Maybe 180 lines of Python.

Manually, I'd spend 40 minutes on API docs alone. Then debugging auth. Then figuring out the response schema. Then writing the scoring logic. Then testing edge cases.

With Claude Code, I described the pipeline in plain English, pointed it at the existing codebase for conventions, and watched it write, test, and fix its own bugs.

The part that changed my workflow permanently: it reads my existing code first. It matched my naming conventions, used my existing database helper, and followed the patterns already in the repo. No "let me refactor your whole project" energy. Just... built the thing that fits.

I run about 30 scripts in production now that were built this way. Enrichment, email warmup monitoring, content scheduling, CRM hygiene. Each one took under 15 minutes to build.

The gap isn't about typing speed. It's about eliminating the research and debugging loops that eat 80% of development time.
posts.cta: If you're still writing every line manually for ops scripts, try timing yourself on the next one. The delta is jarring.

remixes.body:
The slowest part of writing an ops script was never the coding. It was the reading.

I realized this after timing myself on a CRM enrichment pipeline. Out of two hours of "coding," I spent maybe 25 minutes actually writing logic. The rest was API documentation. Digging through response schemas. Finding the right auth flow. Figuring out pagination quirks.

Claude Code collapsed that entire reading phase into about three minutes. Not because it writes faster. Because it already knows the API surface. It's read the docs. It knows that Attio's list endpoint returns nested objects. It knows the enrichment provider's auth is header-based, not query-param.

The script was 180 lines of Python. The logic itself was simple. Pull companies, hit an API, score results, write back. Any competent developer could write it. The question was never ability. It was time-to-first-working-version.

11 minutes vs. 2 hours isn't about the script. It's about eliminating the reconnaissance phase entirely. Every ops script has this hidden cost. The code is the easy part. The context acquisition is the bottleneck.

I don't use Claude Code because I can't write Python. I use it because I don't want to spend 40 minutes learning a pagination scheme I'll use once.
remixes.cta: Next time you build an integration script, notice how much time is coding vs. reading docs. That ratio is exactly where AI coding tools create leverage.

remixes.hook: I have a rule now: if I can describe a script in plain English in under 60 seconds, Claude Code builds it.
remixes.body:
I have a rule now: if I can describe a script in plain English in under 60 seconds, Claude Code builds it.

Not because I'm lazy. Because I ran the numbers on my own time.

Last month I tracked every ops script I wrote. CRM syncs, data enrichment, report generators, webhook handlers. Fourteen scripts total. Average time when I wrote them manually: 1 hour 45 minutes. Average time when I described them to Claude Code: 14 minutes.

That's not a small gap. That's the difference between "I'll get to it this afternoon" and "done before my coffee's cold."

The scripts that benefit most share three traits. They touch external APIs with documented schemas. They follow patterns I've built before (extract, transform, load). And they don't require novel algorithmic thinking.

That last point matters. Claude Code isn't replacing my hard engineering work. It's replacing my repetitive engineering work. The auth boilerplate. The retry logic. The CSV formatting. The stuff I've written a hundred times and will write a hundred more.

The rule has a corollary too. If I can't describe it in 60 seconds, that's a signal the problem isn't well-defined yet. And poorly defined problems produce bad code regardless of who writes it, human or AI.

The 60-second rule isn't about speed. It's about clarity.
remixes.cta: Try this for a week: if you can describe the script in under 60 seconds, let the AI build it. Track how many hours you reclaim.

posts.title: AI engineer role is a trap
posts.hook: Companies hiring "AI engineers" without defining the role are about to waste $180k.
posts.body:
Companies hiring "AI engineers" without defining the role are about to waste $180k.

I've talked to three founders this month who posted AI engineer roles. When I asked what the person would own, I got three different answers:

"Prompt optimization" (that's a Tuesday afternoon task, not a role)
"Building our AI features" (so... a software engineer)
"Figuring out where AI fits" (that's a strategy consultant)

The problem is that AI capability is collapsing into existing roles faster than companies can create new ones. Your backend engineer should know how to call an LLM API. Your data person should know how to build an eval pipeline. Your ops person should know how to wire up an agent for workflow automation.

The companies I see executing well aren't hiring AI engineers. They're upskilling their existing team and giving them Claude Code or Cursor licenses. One founder I work with gave every engineer on his 6-person team a Claude Code subscription. Their shipping velocity doubled in two weeks. Cost: $1,200/month. Savings vs. hiring a dedicated AI engineer: $170k+/year.

The role that actually makes sense is "AI-native engineer" as a modifier on existing functions, not a standalone title with an ambiguous mandate.
posts.cta: Before you post that AI engineer req, write down the first three deliverables. If you can't, the role doesn't exist yet.

remixes.hook: If your AI engineer's first deliverable is a "proof of concept," you just hired a researcher with no deadline.
remixes.body:
If your AI engineer's first deliverable is a "proof of concept," you just hired a researcher with no deadline.

I've been reviewing AI hiring plans for early-stage companies. The pattern is consistent and expensive. Founder reads about AI transformation. Founder decides they need an AI person. Founder writes a job description that's basically "figure out AI for us." Salary: $160-200k.

Three months later, they have a Jupyter notebook with a demo, a slide deck explaining transformer architecture, and zero production features.

The problem isn't the hire. It's the scope. "AI engineer" without clear deliverables is a blank check. And blank checks in startups don't buy outcomes. They buy exploration.

The companies I've seen get this right do something specific. They don't hire an AI engineer. They identify one workflow that's painful, manual, and data-rich. Then they hire someone to automate that workflow. The title might say AI engineer, but the job description says "reduce manual review time by 60% in Q1."

That's a deliverable. That's measurable. That person knows if they're succeeding or failing by week four.

The $180k "figure out AI" hire doesn't know if they're succeeding until someone decides they're not. Usually around month six. Usually after they've built three demos that never shipped.
remixes.cta: Before you hire for AI, write down the workflow you want automated and the metric you'll measure. The role writes itself after that.

remixes.body:
"AI engineer" is the new "growth hacker." A trendy title hiding the fact that nobody knows what the job actually is.

Remember growth hackers? Every startup needed one in 2015. Nobody could agree on what they did. Some were marketers. Some were engineers. Some were PMs who ran A/B tests. The title meant everything and nothing simultaneously.

AI engineer is following the same trajectory. I talked to three founders this month who were hiring for the role. Their definitions:

Founder A: "Someone to optimize our prompts." That's a task, not a job. Any engineer on your team can learn this in a week.

Founder B: "Building AI features into our product." So you need a software engineer who knows how to call an API. You already have those.

Founder C: "Figuring out our AI strategy." That's a consultant engagement, not a full-time role. And it should take 6 weeks, not 6 months.

The common thread: none of these founders needed a new role. They needed clarity on what they were trying to build. The AI engineer title was a shortcut around that clarity. "We don't know what we need, so let's hire someone smart and let them figure it out."

That approach burns $180k and produces slide decks. Every time.

Define the outcome first. The role follows.
remixes.cta: Search your company's open reqs for any title that didn't exist two years ago. Ask: do we have a deliverable or just a buzzword?

posts.title: Multi-agent token costs are brutal
posts.hook: My 3-agent enrichment pipeline was burning $47/day before I noticed. One architectural change dropped it to $6.
posts.body:
My 3-agent enrichment pipeline was burning $47/day before I noticed. One architectural change dropped it to $6.

posts.title: AI SDRs expose fake sellers
posts.hook: AI SDRs didn't kill sales jobs. They revealed which ones were already dead.
posts.body:
AI SDRs didn't kill sales jobs. They revealed which ones were already dead.

I built outbound infrastructure for companies where the "sales process" was: buy a list, blast 10,000 emails, pray for replies, call the 2% who respond. That entire workflow is now automatable. And the people who only knew how to execute that workflow are panicking.

But the reps I've seen thrive alongside AI outbound share a pattern. They do the thing the machine can't: they build relationships in rooms the AI can't enter. They read body language on a Zoom call. They know when a prospect's "we're evaluating options" means "our budget got cut" vs. "I need air cover from my boss."

The split is getting clearer every month. Reps who were essentially human mail-merge machines are being replaced by actual mail-merge machines. Reps who understand buyer psychology, who can navigate a 6-person buying committee, who can create urgency without being sleazy... those people are more valuable than ever.

I came from trades. Plumbing. The guys who thrived weren't the ones who could dig a trench faster. They were the ones who could walk into a house, diagnose the real problem, and explain it so the homeowner trusted them.

Same energy. Different industry.
posts.cta: If your entire sales motion can be replaced by a sequence, the sequence was always the job. Time to evolve the job.

The work that requires reading a room, not reading a spreadsheet.

: group one was always vulnerable. Not because of AI. Because their entire value proposition was executing a process that didn't require human judgment. AI just made that obvious faster than normal market pressure would have.

The reps who build pipeline through relationships, pattern recognition, and creative problem-solving are more valuable now than before. Because AI handles everything else.

posts.title: Smaller lists win cold email
posts.hook: My best cold email campaign this year was 143 contacts. 9 meetings booked. 6.3% conversion.
posts.body:
My best cold email campaign this year was 143 contacts. 9 meetings booked. 6.3% conversion.

My worst was 2,400 contacts. 4 meetings. 0.17%.

The difference wasn't copy. Wasn't subject lines. Wasn't send time optimization. It was list quality.

The 143-contact list took 6 hours to build. I pulled companies showing specific hiring signals from job boards, cross-referenced with tech stack data from enrichment APIs, filtered to companies in a 90-day buying window based on funding data, then manually reviewed every single one.

The 2,400-contact list took 20 minutes. Downloaded from Apollo with basic firmographic filters. "SaaS, 50-200 employees, US." Done.

The small list had a 68% open rate because every email referenced something real about the company. The large list had a 31% open rate with generic personalization that read like... generic personalization.

This is where coding agents changed the math for me. Building a hyper-targeted list used to be a full-day manual grind. Now I have enrichment scripts that pull signals from 4 sources, score against ICP criteria, and output a ranked list in under an hour. The bottleneck moved from "can I afford to be selective" to "how selective can I get."

Smaller list. More research per contact. Higher conversion. Lower cost per meeting. The math works every time.
posts.cta: Try cutting your next campaign list by 80% and spending that saved time on research per account. Track the conversion delta.

Cold email math is broken because people optimize the wrong variable.

Everyone A/B tests subject lines. Everyone tweaks send times. Everyone rotates domains. These are rounding errors.

The only variable that moves conversion by 10x or more is who you're emailing in the first place.

I ran two campaigns back to back. Same copy. Same offer. Same sender reputation. Campaign A went to a curated list of 143 accounts showing active buying signals. Hiring for the role my product supports. Tech stack that creates the problem I solve. Recent funding that gives them budget. Campaign B went to 2,400 contacts scraped from a loose ICP filter.

Campaign A: 6.3% meeting rate. Campaign B: 0.17%.

That's not a marginal difference. That's a completely different business model. One turns cold email into a predictable pipeline channel. The other turns it into expensive spam.

: building a great list is slow, manual, and boring. It took me 6 hours to build those 143 contacts. Most of that was reading job posts, checking LinkedIn activity, and cross-referencing tech stack data. Nobody wants to do that work. Which is exactly why it works so well when you do.
remixes.cta: Next campaign, build your list like you're hand-picking a dinner party guest list. The conversion rate will tell you whether you got it right.

remixes.label: anti-scale-playbook
remixes.hook: I deliberately made my outbound campaigns smaller this year. Revenue went up.
remixes.body:
I deliberately made my outbound campaigns smaller this year. Revenue went up.

Q1 I was running the standard playbook. Big lists, automated sequences, volume metrics on a dashboard. Looked impressive. 3,000 contacts per month going through the machine. Meeting rate hovering around 0.2%.

Then I flipped it. Capped every campaign at 200 contacts max. Spent the time I would have spent managing volume on actually researching each account. What are they hiring for? What tools are they using? What did their last quarterly earnings call say about the problem I solve?

The results were immediate and honestly a little embarrassing given how long I ran the volume play. Meetings per campaign went from 4-5 to 8-12. Show rates improved because the prospects were actually qualified. Close rates improved because I walked into calls already knowing their situation.

Smaller lists also fixed deliverability. Fewer sends meant cleaner sender reputation. Reply rates went up, which trained the inbox algorithms to trust my domain.

The whole outbound motion got simpler. Fewer contacts to manage. Fewer follow-ups. Fewer "not interested" replies clogging the pipeline. More actual conversations with people who had the problem and the budget.
remixes.cta: Pick your weakest-performing campaign. Cut the list to your top 15%. Rewrite the first line for each one. Run it again and compare.

posts.title: CRM graveyard is a goldmine
posts.hook: We found $340k in reactivatable pipeline sitting in closed-lost records nobody had touched in 14 months.
posts.body:
We found $340k in reactivatable pipeline sitting in closed-lost records nobody had touched in 14 months.

The play was simple. Pulled every closed-lost deal from the last 18 months. Enriched each one with current signals: did they hire for the role that blocked the deal? Did they raise funding? Did the champion change companies? Did the competitor they chose show churn signals?

Out of 847 closed-lost records, 112 had at least one reactivation signal. Of those, 43 had two or more signals stacking.

We ran a 3-touch sequence to the 43. Personalized to the specific signal. "Saw you just brought on a VP of Revenue Ops. When we talked last March, not having that role was the blocker. Wondering if the conversation looks different now."

11 replied. 7 took meetings. 3 are in active pipeline right now.

The CRM isn't just a record of what happened. It's a map of future timing. Every closed-lost deal has a reason it was lost. Most of those reasons are temporal, not permanent. Budget wasn't there. Wrong stakeholder. Competing priority. These things change.

I built a script that runs weekly now. Pulls closed-lost, enriches against signal sources, flags anything with 2+ reactivation indicators. Takes 4 minutes to run. The pipeline it surfaces is warmer than any cold outbound I've ever sent.
posts.cta: Your CRM graveyard is probably your highest-ROI prospecting channel. The leads already know you. They just need a reason to re-engage.

212 showed at least one re-engagement signal. We ran a targeted sequence to those 212. Personal, referencing the original deal and the new signal. 34 replied. 11 booked meetings. We found $340k in reactivatable pipeline.

The cost of this play was basically zero. The data was already in the CRM. The enrichment tools were already in the stack. The only thing missing was someone actually doing it.

posts.title: Build in public revenue math
posts.hook: Building in public isn't a marketing strategy. It's a trust compression engine.
posts.body:
Building in public isn't a marketing strategy. It's a trust compression engine.

When someone discovers your product through an ad, they need 7-12 touches before they'll consider buying. When someone has been watching you build for three months, reading your wins and failures, seeing the actual product evolve in real time... they show up to the first call pre-sold.

I track this. My build-in-public leads close 3x faster than cold leads. Average sales cycle: 8 days vs. 26 days. They skip the "prove you're legit" phase because they already watched me prove it, publicly, for months.

The part most people get wrong: they treat building in public like a content calendar. Monday is metrics, Wednesday is lessons, Friday is wins. That cadence makes you a newsletter. Not a builder.

What works is posting when something actually happens. Shipped a feature? Post. Broke production? Post. Lost a customer and learned why? Post. The irregularity is the authenticity signal. Nobody building real things ships on a content calendar schedule.

The other mistake: vanity metrics as proof of progress. "Hit 1,000 followers" means nothing to a buyer. "Reduced enrichment costs from $2,400/mo to $180/mo by building it myself" is a proof point that makes your ICP lean in.

Show the work. Show the numbers. Show the failures. That's the whole strategy.
posts.cta: If you're building something, the build log is your best sales asset. Start sharing it.

A prospect who finds you through an ad is starting from zero trust. They need to evaluate your credibility, understand your product, verify your claims, and build enough confidence to risk a meeting. That process takes 7-12 touchpoints. Weeks to months.

A prospect who has been following your build log for three months has already done all of that passively. They've seen your product evolve. They've watched you solve real problems. They've read your honest assessments of what works and what doesn't. By the time they reach out, they're not evaluating. They're confirming.

I track this. Build-in-public sourced leads convert to meetings at 68%. Ad-sourced leads convert at 22%. The sales cycle is roughly half as long. They ask fewer "prove it" questions because they've already seen the proof.

The mechanism isn't mysterious. Trust normally requires repeated interactions over time. Building in public compresses those interactions into content consumption. Someone reading your weekly build updates for 12 weeks has had more meaningful exposure to your thinking than someone who sat through three sales calls.

The catch: it only works if you share real information. Wins and losses. Actual metrics. Honest assessments. The moment you start curating for appearance, you lose the trust compression effect.
remixes.cta: Start logging your build decisions publicly. Not polished case studies. Raw notes on what you tried, what worked, what didn't. That's the content your future buyers are looking for.

posts.title: Saturday afternoon shipping culture
posts.hook: I shipped a full prospect scoring pipeline last Saturday between lunch and dinner. Two years ago that would have been a two-week sprint.
posts.body:
I shipped a full prospect scoring pipeline last Saturday between lunch and dinner. Two years ago that would have been a two-week sprint.

The build: pull ICP criteria from Attio, run each prospect through 4 enrichment sources, apply a weighted scoring model, write results back to CRM with explanations, trigger a Slack alert for anything scoring above 80.

Claude Code wrote the initial pipeline. I described the scoring logic in plain English, pointed it at my existing enrichment modules, and it produced working code that followed my project conventions. I spent most of my time on the scoring weights, not the code.

Total lines of code: ~240. Total time debugging: maybe 20 minutes, mostly edge cases around missing enrichment data.

This is the part of the "AI replaces developers" discourse that misses the point. The AI didn't replace me. It eliminated the mechanical translation step between "I know exactly what I want" and "it exists as working code." The thinking, the architecture decisions, the domain knowledge of what signals actually predict buying intent... that's still mine.

What changed is the gap between idea and implementation. It used to be weeks. Now it's hours. That means I can test more ideas, kill bad ones faster, and iterate on the ones that work.

Every founder should be building like this. Not because coding agents are magic. Because the cost of experimenting just dropped by 90%.

remixes.body:
The prospect scoring pipeline I built on Saturday would have cost $15k from an agency and taken 6 weeks. It took me 4 hours and a Claude Code subscription.

This isn't about being a better engineer. I'm not. Two years ago I couldn't have built this in two weeks, let alone an afternoon. The tooling changed.

Here's what I built between lunch and dinner: pull ICP criteria from Attio, run each prospect through 4 enrichment sources, apply a weighted scoring model, write results back to CRM with human-readable explanations for each score, trigger a Slack alert for anything above 80.

The workflow: I described what I wanted in plain English. Claude Code wrote the initial pipeline. I tested it against 10 known-good prospects to validate the scoring logic. Adjusted the weights based on what the model got wrong. Ran it against the full database. Total time from "I should build this" to "it's running in production": about 4 hours.

The economics of building internal tools have fundamentally shifted. Things that used to require a dedicated sprint or an outside vendor are now Saturday projects. Not because the problems got simpler. Because the gap between "I know what I want" and "it exists and works" collapsed.

This changes the calculus on what's worth building. When the build cost drops by 90%, a lot of "nice to have" tools become "obviously we should have this."

remixes.label: founder-leverage-shift
remixes.hook: Two years ago I had ideas and no way to ship them fast. Now I have a build backlog I'm actually burning through.
remixes.body:
Two years ago I had ideas and no way to ship them fast. Now I have a build backlog I'm actually burning through.

Every founder has a list of things they'd build "if they had time" or "if they had a technical co-founder" or "if they could justify the sprint." Prospect scoring. Automated reporting. Signal detection pipelines. Internal dashboards. All the operational infrastructure that separates a company running on intuition from one running on data.

That list used to be aspirational. Now it's a Saturday afternoon.

Last weekend I shipped a full prospect scoring pipeline. Pulls criteria from the CRM, enriches through four data sources, scores with a weighted model, writes results back with explanations, alerts on high scores. Four hours. Working in production by dinner.

The week before, I built an automated competitive monitoring system. Tracks competitor pricing pages, job posts, and product changelog updates. Alerts me when something changes. Two hours.

This isn't about the specific tools. It's about what happens to a business when the founder can ship operational infrastructure at this speed. Problems that used to persist for months because "we'll get to it next quarter" get solved the same day they're identified.

The founders who figure out how to leverage AI coding tools for internal operations are going to pull away fast. Not because of one tool. Because of the compound effect of solving 50 small operational problems that their competitors are still living with.
remixes.cta: What operational problem has your team been working around for months? The build cost probably dropped 90% since you last estimated it. Revisit it.

tones.builder:
I shipped a full prospect scoring pipeline last Saturday between lunch and dinner. Two years ago that would have been a two-week sprint.

The build: pull ICP criteria from Attio, run each prospect through 4 enrichment sources, apply a weighted scoring model, write results back to CRM with explanations, trigger a Slack alert for anything scoring above 80.

Claude Code wrote the initial pipeline. I described the scoring logic in plain English, pointed it at my existing enrichment modules, and it produced working code that followed my project conventions. I spent most of my time on the scoring weights, not the code.

Total lines of code: ~240. Total time debugging: maybe 20 minutes, mostly edge cases around missing enrichment data.

This is the part of the "AI replaces developers" discourse that misses the point. The AI didn't replace me. It eliminated the mechanical translation step between "I know exactly what I want" and "it exists as working code." The thinking, the architecture decisions, the domain knowledge of what signals actually predict buying intent... that's still mine.

What changed is the gap between idea and implementation. It used to be weeks. Now it's hours. That means I can test more ideas, kill bad ones faster, and iterate on the ones that work.

Every founder should be building like this. Not because coding agents are magic. Because the cost of experimenting just dropped by 90%.
